facts.claim: "Tangerine" by Noah Richardson was released as a single on May 26, 2023 and runs 3:30.
Credits list Noah Ward Richardson as lyricist, composer and producer, with the label given as 2971105 Records DK2.
In a podcast interview, Richardson said "Tangerine" was one of the first ~25 songs he wrote and that it existed on SoundCloud in 2021 before being redone because people liked it.
A review describes the song as exploring fleeting moments with a past lover, tying together senses through small, intimate details such as hair left in bedsheets.
The song went viral on TikTok and reached Spotify's Viral 50 in the US, Canada and UK, with nearly 12M streams across platforms according to First Avenue's bio.
A 2026 concert report says "Tangerine" reached the Top 10 charts in the US, UK and Canada and has passed 15 million Spotify streams.
Richardson is a Philadelphia alt singer-songwriter who began as a street performer in Philly.
He is described as known for a 'funeral rock' style drawing on his upbringing in a funeral home, and he has been involved with NBC's The Voice.
Richardson used to record in the basement of his family's funeral home in Philadelphia.
His other 2023 singles include "7 Minutes in Heaven", "Don't Leave Me" and "I Don't Wanna Fall In Love Again", and he released the album "Dead To Me" in 2022.

research.lineage: The song sits in the TikTok-era folk-influenced indie and alt-pop singer-songwriter scene, promoted alongside visuals of Hozier and Dominic Fike.

draft:
The toothpaste is the detail that does it. Plenty of breakup songs inventory what a lover left behind, but **"Tangerine"** lands on the most ordinary object in the bathroom and turns it into a small act of self-harm: "No brush but you left your toothpaste / So I won't forget how you taste." The narrator isn't just stumbling over leftovers. They're keeping them on purpose, so the wound stays fresh.

That's the feeling at the center of Noah Richardson's song, and he doesn't pretend it's healthy. The chorus names hair still caught in the bedsheets, a scent like the fruit in the title, and then a line that admits the whole thing outright: "Addicted to you and your misery." Right before it, the narrator claims to be doing what they can to come clean. Both stay true at once, the wanting-to-quit and the reaching for another hit, and the song never settles which one wins. One review of the track put it well, describing how it ties the senses together through small, intimate details. Smell, touch, taste: the ex is gone, but the body hasn't caught up.

The verses carry a quieter tug-of-war. The narrator casts the other person as the heartbreaker who's too good at leaving, and casts themself as the storm chaser who keeps believing. It's a flattering self-portrait, loyalty dressed up as daring. By the second verse the swagger cracks into plain hurt: the lover is a sorceress, the narrator is tortured, and they wonder why it was so hard to see. The sharpest turn is a single word. The first verse ends with the two of them walking away. The second insists they won't. Then the chorus comes back doubled at the end, the same images circling, like someone who can't stop rereading old texts.

The sound keeps all this in a relaxed sway rather than a wail. A clean electric guitar picks out an arpeggiated figure with a touch of delay, over a simple bass line and a laid-back, mid-tempo kit with a prominent snare. Richardson's voice is mid-range and a little nasal, unfussy, and a harmony a third above gives the hook a warmer glow. The production is clean and polished with a natural room around it. It's easy to see why the song caught fire on TikTok and reached Spotify's Viral 50 in the US, Canada and the UK, landing in the same folk-tinged alt-pop lane as Hozier and Dominic Fike.

It wasn't built for that moment, though. Richardson, a Philadelphia songwriter who started out busking on the city's streets and used to record in the basement of his family's funeral home, has said "Tangerine" was among his first two dozen or so songs. It sat on SoundCloud in 2021 before he redid it because people kept loving it. He wrote, composed and produced it himself.

The song sticks because it catches the part of grief nobody admits to: you could throw the toothpaste away, and you don't.

factCheck.claim: Lyric quote: "No brush but you left your toothpaste / So I won't forget how you taste."
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly, and the two lines are consecutive.

factCheck.claim: The lover is a sorceress, the narrator is tortured, and they wonder why it was so hard to see
factCheck.note: The lyric is "Was it so hard to tell", not "see". Wording fixed. Also, this stanza is not literally the "second verse", so that framing was loosened.

factCheck.claim: First verse ends with the two of them walking away; the second insists they won't
factCheck.note: The lyrics support "walk away" in the opening stanza and "we won't walk away" later. The verse numbering was loosened to match the lyric structure.
